claim: C. elegans has a nervous system of only 302 neurons.
source: Here we show that the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans can discriminate spatial patterns in its surroundings, despite having a nervous system of only 302 neurons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about C. elegans neuroanatomy.

claim: C. elegans can discriminate spatial patterns in its surroundings.
source: Here we show that the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans can discriminate spatial patterns in its surroundings, despite having a nervous system of only 302 neurons.
evidence: This is the primary finding demonstrated through behavioral experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Spatial pattern selectivity in C. elegans requires touch-dependent dopamine signaling.
source: This spatial pattern selectivity requires touch-dependent dopamine signaling, including the mechanosensory TRP-4 channel in dopaminergic neurons and the D2-like dopamine receptor DOP-3.
evidence: Supported by genetic and behavioral experiments showing requirement of dopamine pathway components.

claim: Spatial pattern selectivity requires the mechanosensory TRP-4 channel in dopaminergic neurons.
source: This spatial pattern selectivity requires touch-dependent dopamine signaling, including the mechanosensory TRP-4 channel in dopaminergic neurons and the D2-like dopamine receptor DOP-3.
evidence: Demonstrated through mutant analysis and cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Spatial pattern selectivity requires the D2-like dopamine receptor DOP-3.
source: This spatial pattern selectivity requires touch-dependent dopamine signaling, including the mechanosensory TRP-4 channel in dopaminergic neurons and the D2-like dopamine receptor DOP-3.
evidence: Demonstrated through mutant analysis showing dop-3 mutants have reduced pattern preference.

claim: Spatial pattern selectivity varies significantly among C. elegans wild isolates.
source: We find that spatial pattern selectivity varies significantly among C. elegans wild isolates.
evidence: Demonstrated by testing multiple wild isolates in the spatial pattern preference assay.

claim: Natural variations in TRP-4 reduce the mechanosensitivity of dopaminergic neurons.
source: Electrophysiological recordings show that natural variations in TRP-4 reduce the mechanosensitivity of dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings comparing N2 and HW strains.

claim: Polymorphic substitutions in TRP-4 alter the selectivity of spatial patterns.
source: Polymorphic substitutions in either TRP-4 or DOP-3 alter the selectivity of spatial patterns.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of wild isolates and rescue experiments with different TRP-4 variants.

claim: Polymorphic substitutions in DOP-3 alter the selectivity of spatial patterns.
source: Polymorphic substitutions in either TRP-4 or DOP-3 alter the selectivity of spatial patterns.
evidence: Demonstrated through CRISPR editing of the A273G substitution in N2 worms.

claim: Dopamine signaling has an ancestral role in tuning spatial pattern preferences in simple nervous systems.
source: Together, these results demonstrate an ancestral role for dopamine signaling in tuning spatial pattern preferences in a simple nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings in C. elegans, a simple model organism.

claim: C. elegans feeds and reproduces in decomposing fruits and plant stems.
source: To address this question, we investigated the roundworm C. elegans, which feeds and reproduces in decomposing fruits and plant stems (Barrière and Félix, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrière and Félix, 2014.

claim: C. elegans lacks vision and hearing.
source: C. elegans has only 302 neurons and lack vision and hearing, mainly relying on smell and touch to sense their environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans sensory capabilities.

claim: C. elegans mainly relies on smell and touch to sense their environment.
source: C. elegans has only 302 neurons and lack vision and hearing, mainly relying on smell and touch to sense their environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans sensory modalities.

claim: Touch to the worm body or nose elicits reflex withdrawal responses.
source: For example, touch to the worm body or nose elicits reflex withdrawal responses (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981, Chalfie and Wolinsky, 1990; Kaplan and Horvitz, 1993; Sulston et al., 1975; Way and Chalfie, 1989), which allows the worms to quickly avoid potential danger.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanosensory detection of food elicits a slowing in C. elegans locomotion.
source: Indeed, mechanosensory detection of food elicits a slowing in C. elegans locomotion, increasing the time spent where food is present (Sawin et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawin et al., 2000.

claim: The Bristol N2 strain exhibits a strong preference for pattern IV.
source: We found that the Bristol N2 strain exhibits a strong preference for pattern IV (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Approximately 63% of N2 worms were found in pattern IV 60 min after entering the chamber.
source: Approximately 63% of N2 worms were found in the section containing pattern IV 60 min after entering the chamber.
evidence: Quantitative data from behavioral experiments.

claim: Only 9–15% of N2 worms were found in each of the sections I, II and III.
source: By contrast, we observed only 9–15% of worms in each of the other sections I, II and III (Figure 1C) with lower pillar densities.
evidence: Quantitative data from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pattern IV preference was very stable between 60 and 90 min.
source: Pattern IV preference was very stable between 60 and 90 min, but was reduced at 120 min.
evidence: Demonstrated by time course experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pattern IV preference was reduced at 120 min.
source: Pattern IV preference was very stable between 60 and 90 min, but was reduced at 120 min.
evidence: Demonstrated by time course experiments.

claim: The decrease in pattern IV preference at 120 min was likely due to starvation.
source: This decrease was likely due to starvation, as addition of food (OP50 bacteria) into the chamber prolonged the preference for pattern IV, which lasted at least 180 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inference supported by experiments showing food addition prolongs preference.

claim: Addition of food into the chamber prolonged the preference for pattern IV to at least 180 min.
source: This decrease was likely due to starvation, as addition of food (OP50 bacteria) into the chamber prolonged the preference for pattern IV, which lasted at least 180 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with food addition shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Worms that had already been starved prior to the experiment exhibited a significant reduction in pattern IV preference.
source: Consistent with this notion, worms that had already been starved prior to the experiment exhibited a significant reduction in pattern IV preference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that feeding state (starvation) can override an inherent preference for pattern selectivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with pre-starved worms shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Feeding state (starvation) can override an inherent preference for pattern selectivity.
source: Consistent with this notion, worms that had already been starved prior to the experiment exhibited a significant reduction in pattern IV preference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that feeding state (starvation) can override an inherent preference for pattern selectivity.
evidence: Inference drawn from starvation experiments.

claim: Single-worm pattern preference index values were similar to those obtained in population experiments.
source: Single-worm pattern preference index values were similar to those obtained in population experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating that pattern selectivity is an individual rather than group behavior.
evidence: Demonstrated by single-worm analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pattern selectivity is an individual rather than group behavior.
source: Single-worm pattern preference index values were similar to those obtained in population experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating that pattern selectivity is an individual rather than group behavior.
evidence: Inference from single-worm versus population experiments.

claim: C. elegans exhibits aggregation behavior at optimal oxygen levels.
source: C. elegans exhibits aggregation behavior at optimal oxygen levels (Cheung et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2004 and Gray et al., 2004.

claim: gcy-35 mutant worms lack the GCY-35 soluble guanylate cyclase and are defective in oxygen-dependent aggregation, bordering, and social feeding behaviors.
source: To this end, we tested mutant worms that lack the GCY-35 soluble guanylate cyclase and are defective in oxygen-dependent aggregation, bordering, and social feeding behaviors (Cheung et al., 2004; Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2004 and Gray et al., 2004.

claim: gcy-35 mutant worms continued to show preference for pattern IV.
source: However, these mutant gcy-35 worms continued to show preference for pattern IV (Figure 1D), indicating that pattern IV selectivity was independent of possible variations in oxygen levels and oxygen sensing.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with gcy-35 mutants shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pattern IV selectivity is independent of possible variations in oxygen levels and oxygen sensing.
source: However, these mutant gcy-35 worms continued to show preference for pattern IV (Figure 1D), indicating that pattern IV selectivity was independent of possible variations in oxygen levels and oxygen sensing.
evidence: Inference from gcy-35 mutant experiments.

claim: Mutant worms with dysfunctional MEC-10 DEG/ENaC channels showed a significant reduction in their preference for pattern IV.
source: By contrast, mutant worms with dysfunctional MEC-10 DEG/ENaC channels showed a significant reduction in their preference for pattern IV (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with mec-10 mutants shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Single-copy Pmec-10::mec-10 transgenes that drive MEC-10 expression in the six touch receptor neurons and in PVD and FLP neurons fully restored the preference for pattern IV.
source: As expected, single-copy Pmec-10::mec-10 transgenes that drive MEC-10 expression in the six touch receptor neurons and in PVD and FLP neurons fully restored the preference for pattern IV.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of MEC-10 under Pegl-44 in FLP and HSN neurons rescued the defects in mec-10(tm1552) mutant worms.
source: Expression of MEC-10 under Pegl-44 in FLP and HSN neurons (Wu et al., 2001) also rescued the defects in mec-10(tm1552) mutant worms.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-specific rescue experiments, with citation to Wu et al., 2001 for promoter specificity.

claim: MEC-10 expression in the six touch receptor neurons (driven by Pmec-18) did not recover the preference for pattern IV.
source: By contrast, MEC-10 expression in the six touch receptor neurons (driven by Pmec-18) did not recover the preference for pattern IV.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: MEC-10 acts in the polymodal nociceptive FLP neurons to support the selection of pattern IV.
source: Together, these data indicate that MEC-10 acts in the polymodal nociceptive FLP neurons to support the selection of pattern IV.
evidence: Inference from cell-specific rescue experiments showing rescue with Pegl-44 but not Pmec-18.

claim: In a chamber consisting of patterns I and III only, N2 worms showed a clear preference for pattern III.
source: To determine whether pattern selectivity depends on the particular absolute pillar density of pattern IV, we used a chamber consisting of patterns I and III only (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). In this chamber, N2 worms showed a clear preference for pattern III (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), even though this is a non-favored pattern in the quad-chamber.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments in a two-pattern chamber shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Pattern selectivity is based on comparison between different spatial patterns rather than on the specific structural arrangement of pattern IV.
source: We therefore conclude that pattern selectivity is based on comparison between different spatial patterns i.e., environmental context, rather than on the specific structural arrangement of pattern IV.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing preference for pattern III in a two-pattern chamber.

claim: Worms that left pattern IV and entered pattern III re-crossed back into pattern IV at a much higher rate than worms already within pattern IV.
source: We tracked worms that left pattern IV and entered into the less desired pattern III (Figure 2A), and found that these worms re-crossed back into the preferred pattern IV at a much higher rate than worms already within pattern IV (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by tracking experiments shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: There is an increase in both reversal and turning rates when worms cross the IV-to-III boundary.
source: We also found an increase in both reversal and turning rates when worms cross the IV-to-III boundary (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Worms sense local changes in pattern density and respond quickly to unfavorable changes by reorientation.
source: Therefore, worms sense local changes in pattern density, and respond quickly to unfavorable changes by reorientation, reinforcing our finding of their ability to make decisions based on comparisons of spatial density.
evidence: Inference from boundary crossing experiments showing increased reversal and turning rates.

claim: Worms in pattern IV of the quad-chamber moved more slowly and paused more than worms in the uni-chamber.
source: We found that worms in pattern IV of the quad-chamber moved more slowly and paused more than worms in the uni-chamber (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by locomotion analysis comparing quad- and uni-chambers shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: Slowing and pausing could prolong the stay of worms in pattern IV.
source: Such slowing and pausing could prolong the stay of worms in pattern IV.
evidence: Logical inference from observed behavioral changes.

claim: The clustering of worms in pattern IV is due to both real-time responses to pattern changes upon boundary crossing and to longer-lasting effects caused by the experience of other less desired patterns.
source: Together, these data suggest that the clustering of worms in pattern IV is due to both real-time responses to pattern changes upon boundary crossing and to longer-lasting effects caused by the experience of other less desired patterns.
evidence: Inference from boundary crossing and locomotion experiments.

claim: Without vision or hearing, C. elegans can take advantage of mechanosensory information to compare and select between spatial patterns in its environment.
source: Thus, without vision or hearing, C. elegans can take advantage of mechanosensory information to compare and select between spatial patterns in its environment.
evidence: Inference from all behavioral experiments demonstrating spatial pattern selectivity.

claim: In C. elegans, dopamine regulates a variety of behaviors including locomotion, mechanosensation, food availability, touch habituation, and the swim-to-crawl transition.
source: In C. elegans, dopamine regulates a variety of behaviors including locomotion, mechanosensation, food availability, touch habituation, and the swim-to-crawl transition (Calhoun et al., 2015; Chase et al., 2004; Hills et al., 2004; Kindt et al., 2007; Sanyal et al., 2004; Sawin et al., 2000; Vidal-Gadea et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Dopamine signals decrease locomotion rates when worms enter a food source.
source: In particular, dopamine signals decrease locomotion rates when worms enter a food source (a lawn of bacteria) (Sawin et al., 2000), and increase returning frequency when worms leave the bacteria lawn (Hills et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawin et al., 2000.

claim: Dopamine signals increase returning frequency when worms leave the bacteria lawn.
source: In particular, dopamine signals decrease locomotion rates when worms enter a food source (a lawn of bacteria) (Sawin et al., 2000), and increase returning frequency when worms leave the bacteria lawn (Hills et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hills et al., 2004.

claim: cat-2(e1112) animals lack the CAT-2 tyrosine hydroxylase and are defective in dopamine biosynthesis.
source: To test whether dopamine is required also for spatial pattern selectivity, we examined cat-2(e1112) animals, which lack the CAT-2 tyrosine hydroxylase and are defective in dopamine biosynthesis (Lints and Emmons, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lints and Emmons, 1999.

claim: cat-2 mutant animals have disrupted pattern selectivity with reduced preference for pattern IV.
source: We observed that cat-2 mutant animals have disrupted pattern selectivity, as they showed reduced preference for pattern IV in the quad-chambers (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with cat-2 mutants shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of exogenous dopamine restored the accumulation of cat-2 mutants within pattern IV.
source: Addition of exogenous dopamine restored the accumulation of cat-2 mutants within pattern IV (Figure 3A), demonstrating that the defect in spatial pattern selectivity of cat-2 mutants is due to the lack of dopamine.
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments with dopamine addition shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The defect in spatial pattern selectivity of cat-2 mutants is due to the lack of dopamine.
source: Addition of exogenous dopamine restored the accumulation of cat-2 mutants within pattern IV (Figure 3A), demonstrating that the defect in spatial pattern selectivity of cat-2 mutants is due to the lack of dopamine.
evidence: Inference from dopamine rescue experiments.

claim: Disrupting the D2-like receptor DOP-3 led to a reduced preference for pattern IV.
source: We found that disrupting the D2-like receptor DOP-3, but not other dopamine receptors (DOP-1, DOP-2, and DOP-4), led to a reduced preference for pattern IV (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with dopamine receptor mutants shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Disrupting other dopamine receptors (DOP-1, DOP-2, and DOP-4) did not lead to reduced preference for pattern IV.
source: We found that disrupting the D2-like receptor DOP-3, but not other dopamine receptors (DOP-1, DOP-2, and DOP-4), led to a reduced preference for pattern IV (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with dopamine receptor mutants shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DOP-3 is expressed in a variety of neurons in the head, ventral cord and tail.
source: DOP-3 is expressed in a variety of neurons in the head, ventral cord and tail (Chase et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chase et al., 2004.

claim: TRP-4 is a stretch receptor expressed in the CEP, ADE, and PDE dopaminergic neurons and the DVA and DVC interneurons.
source: To identify the molecular sensor that links mechanosensation, dopamine, and spatial pattern preference, we studied mutant worms that lack TRP-4, a stretch receptor expressed in the CEP, ADE, and PDE dopaminergic neurons and the DVA and DVC interneurons (Hu et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2010; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2010; Li et al., 2006.

claim: TRP-4 is the pore-forming subunit of mechanotransduction channels.
source: TRP-4 is the pore-forming subunit of mechanotransduction channels (Kang et al., 2010; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang et al., 2010 and Li et al., 2006.

claim: Mutant trp-4(ok1605) worms significantly reduced their preference for pattern IV.
source: Mutant trp-4(ok1605) worms significantly reduced their preference for pattern IV (Figure 3C) and did not show the enhanced returning behavior after crossing the boundary between section IV and III (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with trp-4 mutants shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms did not show the enhanced returning behavior after crossing the boundary between section IV and III.
source: Mutant trp-4(ok1605) worms significantly reduced their preference for pattern IV (Figure 3C) and did not show the enhanced returning behavior after crossing the boundary between section IV and III (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by boundary crossing experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: trp-4(pek220) mutant worms exhibit similar defects as trp-4(ok1605) worms.
source: We found that trp-4(pek220) mutant worms exhibit similar defects as trp-4(ok1605) worms, confirming that the pattern IV preference requires TRP-4.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with a second trp-4 allele.

claim: The pattern IV preference requires TRP-4.
source: We found that trp-4(pek220) mutant worms exhibit similar defects as trp-4(ok1605) worms, confirming that the pattern IV preference requires TRP-4.
evidence: Inference from experiments with two independent trp-4 alleles.

claim: The defects of trp-4 single mutants were similar to trp-4; cat-2 and trp-4; dop-3 double mutants.
source: The defects of trp-4 single mutants were similar to trp-4; cat-2 and trp-4; dop-3 double mutants, indicating that trp-4 acts in the same dopamine pathway as cat-2 and dop-3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: trp-4 acts in the same dopamine pathway as cat-2 and dop-3.
source: The defects of trp-4 single mutants were similar to trp-4; cat-2 and trp-4; dop-3 double mutants, indicating that trp-4 acts in the same dopamine pathway as cat-2 and dop-3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Inference from genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Single-copy transgenes that express TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons restored the preference for pattern IV.
source: Single-copy transgenes that express TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons restored the preference for pattern IV (Figure 3C), further demonstrating a role of TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons in mediating spatial pattern selectivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons mediates spatial pattern selectivity.
source: Single-copy transgenes that express TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons restored the preference for pattern IV (Figure 3C), further demonstrating a role of TRP-4 in dopaminergic neurons in mediating spatial pattern selectivity.
evidence: Inference from cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Natural genetic variations influence how C. elegans interacts with environmental cues such as food, oxygen, microbial pathogens, and neighboring worms.
source: Recent studies have shown that natural genetic variations influence how C. elegans interacts with environmental cues such as food, oxygen, microbial pathogens, and neighboring worms (Bendesky and Bargmann, 2011; Bendesky et al., 2012, 2011; Chang et al., 2011; Persson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hawaiian CB4856 (HW) worms failed to aggregate in pattern IV of the quad-chambers.
source: Interestingly, we found that unlike N2, HW worms failed to aggregate in pattern IV of the quad-chambers (Figure 4A, B), and their returning behavior at boundaries was significantly reduced in comparison to N2 worms (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with HW strain shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: HW worms' returning behavior at boundaries was significantly reduced in comparison to N2 worms.
source: Interestingly, we found that unlike N2, HW worms failed to aggregate in pattern IV of the quad-chambers (Figure 4A, B), and their returning behavior at boundaries was significantly reduced in comparison to N2 worms (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by boundary crossing experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HW worms exhibited similar traveling speed and pause rates in uni- and quad-chambers.
source: In addition, HW worms exhibited similar traveling speed and pause rates in uni- and quad-chambers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that mechanosensory experience had little impact on HW behavior.
evidence: Demonstrated by locomotion analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mechanosensory experience had little impact on HW behavior.
source: In addition, HW worms exhibited similar traveling speed and pause rates in uni- and quad-chambers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that mechanosensory experience had little impact on HW behavior.
evidence: Inference from locomotion experiments comparing uni- and quad-chambers.

claim: The LSJ1 strain showed similar behavior to N2 worms in the spatial pattern preference assay.
source: To test whether this is the case for spatial pattern selectivity, we examined the LSJ1 strain, a sibling of N2 that was cultivated separately after isolation. We found that the LSJ1 strain showed similar behavior to N2 worms in the spatial pattern preference assay (Figure 4B), suggesting that the difference in spatial pattern selectivity is not due to domestication-derived alleles.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with LSJ1 strain shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in spatial pattern selectivity between N2 and HW is not due to domestication-derived alleles.
source: We found that the LSJ1 strain showed similar behavior to N2 worms in the spatial pattern preference assay (Figure 4B), suggesting that the difference in spatial pattern selectivity is not due to domestication-derived alleles.
evidence: Inference from LSJ1 experiments showing similar behavior to N2.

claim: The stretch receptor TRP-4 in the HW strain carries three amino acid substitutions (M36I, G41S, and E67G).
source: Interestingly, the stretch receptor TRP-4 in the HW strain carries three amino acid substitutions (M36I, G41S, and E67G; Figure 5A) (Thompson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: An N2/HW hybrid strain that carries the HW Chromosome I in an N2 background behaved like the HW strain in the spatial pattern preference assay.
source: An N2/HW hybrid strain that carries the HW Chromosome I in an N2 background behaved like the HW strain in the spatial pattern preference assay.
evidence: Demonstrated by chromosome substitution experiments.

claim: Hybrid strains that carry other HW chromosomes (except X) in the N2 background were indistinguishable from N2 worms.
source: However, hybrid strains that carry other HW chromosomes in the N2 background were indistinguishable from N2 worms (Figure 5B), with the exception of those with HW Chromosome X, which showed a minor but significant reduction in the preference for pattern IV.
evidence: Demonstrated by chromosome substitution experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Hybrid strains with HW Chromosome X showed a minor but significant reduction in the preference for pattern IV.
source: However, hybrid strains that carry other HW chromosomes in the N2 background were indistinguishable from N2 worms (Figure 5B), with the exception of those with HW Chromosome X, which showed a minor but significant reduction in the preference for pattern IV.
evidence: Demonstrated by chromosome substitution experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Other gene(s) on Chromosome X may contribute to the polymorphic behavior.
source: These data are consistent with a role of trp-4 in determining the natural variation in spatial pattern selectivity. They also suggest that other gene(s) on Chromosome X may contribute to the polymorphic behavior.
evidence: Inference from chromosome substitution experiments showing effect of Chromosome X.

claim: A RIL strain that carries the N2 trp-4 gene showed preference for pattern IV.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, two RIL strains behaved differently in the spatial pattern preference assay; one that carries the N2 trp-4 gene showed preference for pattern IV, but another one with HW trp-4 did not.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with recombinant inbred lines shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A RIL strain with HW trp-4 did not show preference for pattern IV.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, two RIL strains behaved differently in the spatial pattern preference assay; one that carries the N2 trp-4 gene showed preference for pattern IV, but another one with HW trp-4 did not.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with recombinant inbred lines shown in Figure 5C.

claim: N2 trp-4 cDNA fully restored the selectivity defects of the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms.
source: N2 trp-4 cDNA fully restored the selectivity defects of the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms. By contrast, HW trp-4 cDNA showed only low levels of rescue (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HW trp-4 cDNA showed only low levels of rescue of trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms.
source: N2 trp-4 cDNA fully restored the selectivity defects of the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms. By contrast, HW trp-4 cDNA showed only low levels of rescue (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: N2 TRP-4 is required for the spatial pattern preference observed in the Bristol strains.
source: These data confirm that N2 TRP-4 is required for the spatial pattern preference observed in the Bristol strains.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments showing N2 but not HW TRP-4 rescues the phenotype.

claim: Overexpression of N2 TRP-4 caused HW worms to show spatial pattern selectivity similar to that of N2.
source: Indeed, we found that N2 TRP-4 but not HW TRP-4 overexpression caused HW worms to show spatial pattern selectivity similar to that of N2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by overexpression experiments in HW background shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Overexpression of HW TRP-4 did not cause HW worms to show spatial pattern selectivity similar to N2.
source: Indeed, we found that N2 TRP-4 but not HW TRP-4 overexpression caused HW worms to show spatial pattern selectivity similar to that of N2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by overexpression experiments in HW background shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The substitution of three residues in HW TRP-4 occurs at the N-terminal region that is adjacent to Ankyrin repeats.
source: The substitution of three residues in HW TRP-4 occurs at the N-terminal region that is adjacent to Ankyrin repeats (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A illustrating the location of substitutions.

claim: The Ankyrin repeats of NOMPC (the TRP-4 homologue in flies) directly bind microtubules.
source: In flies, the Ankyrin repeats of NOMPC (the TRP-4 homologue) directly bind microtubules, and they are essential for mechanogating of the NOMPC channels (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: The Ankyrin repeats of NOMPC are essential for mechanogating of the NOMPC channels.
source: In flies, the Ankyrin repeats of NOMPC (the TRP-4 homologue) directly bind microtubules, and they are essential for mechanogating of the NOMPC channels (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: The mechanoreceptor current in CEP neurons is mediated by TRP-4.
source: The mechanoreceptor current in CEP neurons is mediated by TRP-4, and the amplitude of the current depends on the strength of the applied mechanical force.
evidence: Established from previous studies and confirmed by current experiments.

claim: The amplitude of the mechanoreceptor current depends on the strength of the applied mechanical force.
source: The mechanoreceptor current in CEP neurons is mediated by TRP-4, and the amplitude of the current depends on the strength of the applied mechanical force.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings with varying displacement.

claim: A displacement of 0.5 μm was sufficient to elicit TRP-4 mediated current in N2 worms.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Kang et al., 2010), a displacement of 0.5 μm was sufficient to elicit TRP-4 mediated current in N2 worms, and the current was saturated at 3 μm displacement (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B, with citation to Kang et al., 2010.

claim: The TRP-4 mediated current in N2 worms was saturated at 3 μm displacement.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Kang et al., 2010), a displacement of 0.5 μm was sufficient to elicit TRP-4 mediated current in N2 worms, and the current was saturated at 3 μm displacement (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The sensitivity of HW TRP-4 to mechanical stimuli was significantly reduced.
source: Interestingly, the sensitivity of HW TRP-4 to mechanical stimuli was significantly reduced. Larger mechanical displacement was required to generate currents with similar amplitudes (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings comparing N2 and HW shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Larger mechanical displacement was required to generate currents with similar amplitudes in HW compared to N2.
source: Interestingly, the sensitivity of HW TRP-4 to mechanical stimuli was significantly reduced. Larger mechanical displacement was required to generate currents with similar amplitudes (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: When mechanical stimuli are sufficiently strong, the HW TRP-4 is fully active.
source: It is worth noting that, when mechanical stimuli are sufficiently strong, the HW TRP-4 is fully active (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings at high displacement shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A higher density of pillars (novel pattern V) enhanced the enrichment of HW worms.
source: Consistently, we found that an even higher density of pillars (novel pattern V) enhanced the enrichment of HW worms, but not of trp-4(ok1605) mutants (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with denser pattern shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pattern V did not enhance the enrichment of trp-4(ok1605) mutants.
source: Consistently, we found that an even higher density of pillars (novel pattern V) enhanced the enrichment of HW worms, but not of trp-4(ok1605) mutants (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with denser pattern shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Amino acid substitutions in HW TRP-4 reduce the sensitivity to mechanical stimuli, which could subsequently alter spatial pattern perception in HW worms.
source: Together, these findings indicate that amino acid substitutions in HW TRP-4 reduce the sensitivity to mechanical stimuli, which could subsequently alter spatial pattern perception in HW worms.
evidence: Inference from electrophysiological and behavioral experiments.

claim: A single-copy HW TRP-4 transgene failed to restore spatial preference.
source: Interestingly, whereas a single-copy HW TRP-4 transgene failed to restore spatial preference (Figure 5E), it completely rescued swimming/crawling transition in the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that various types of TRP-4 dependent behaviors are tuned to different levels of mechanogating sensitivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A single-copy HW TRP-4 transgene completely rescued swimming/crawling transition in the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms.
source: Interestingly, whereas a single-copy HW TRP-4 transgene failed to restore spatial preference (Figure 5E), it completely rescued swimming/crawling transition in the trp-4(ok1605) mutant worms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that various types of TRP-4 dependent behaviors are tuned to different levels of mechanogating sensitivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by swim-to-crawl transition experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Various types of TRP-4 dependent behaviors are tuned to different levels of mechanogating sensitivity.

claim: Five wild isolates exhibited a spatial preference like N2.
source: We found that five wild isolates exhibited a spatial preference like N2.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with multiple wild isolates.

claim: Two isolates (AB1 and JU397) with substituted residues in TRP-4 exhibited defects in preference for pattern IV.
source: Two isolates (AB1 and JU397) with substituted residues in TRP-4 exhibited defects in preference for pattern IV in the quad-chambers (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments with wild isolates shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The TRP-4 channels in AB1 and JU397 each carry two substitutions (G41S and E67G).
source: The TRP-4 channels in AB1 and JU397 each carry two substitutions (G41S and E67G), suggesting that the third substitution M36I in the HW strain is not required.
evidence: Inference from sequence analysis and behavioral phenotypes.

claim: The third substitution M36I in the HW strain is not required for the behavioral phenotype.
source: The TRP-4 channels in AB1 and JU397 each carry two substitutions (G41S and E67G), suggesting that the third substitution M36I in the HW strain is not required.
evidence: Inference from comparison of substitutions in different strains with similar phenotypes.

claim: CB4854 carries two substitutions (E67G and I152M) in TRP-4.
source: A third isolate (CB4854) also carries two substitutions (E67G and I152M) in TRP-4; however, these worms did not show significant defects in the spatial pattern preference assay (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence analysis and behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CB4854 worms did not show significant defects in the spatial pattern preference assay.
source: A third isolate (CB4854) also carries two substitutions (E67G and I152M) in TRP-4; however, these worms did not show significant defects in the spatial pattern preference assay (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The G41S substitution is the key residue that modulates TRP-4 mechanosensitivity.
source: The most parsimonious explanation is that the G41S substitution is the key residue that modulates TRP-4 mechanosensitivity.
evidence: Inference from comparing substitutions across strains with different phenotypes.

claim: Three wild isolates (CB4853, JU300, and JU322) showed altered spatial pattern selectivity despite having N2-like TRP-4 sequence.
source: Intriguingly, three wild isolates (CB4853, JU300, and JU322) showed altered spatial pattern selectivity despite having N2-like TRP-4 sequence (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral experiments and sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All three strains (CB4853, JU300, and JU322) carry a substituted residue in DOP-3 at the same position (A273G).
source: Closer examination of their genome sequences revealed that all three strains carry a substituted residue in DOP-3 at the same position (A273G).
evidence: Demonstrated by genome sequence analysis.

claim: Edited N2 worms with the A273G substitution in dop-3 lost their spatial pattern selectivity.
source: Upon editing the dop-3 gene in N2 worms using CRISPR/Cas9 (Friedland et al., 2013), we found that the edited worms with the A273G substitution lost their spatial pattern selectivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by CRISPR editing experiments shown in Figure 7B, with citation to Friedland et al., 2013 for the method.

claim: The DOP-3 A273G mutation is sufficient to impair spatial pattern preference even with fully functional TRP-4.
source: These experiments indicate that the DOP-3 A273G mutation is sufficient to impair spatial pattern preference even with fully functional TRP-4.
evidence: Inference from CRISPR editing experiments in N2 background.

claim: The diversity of spatial pattern selectivity may arise from variations in either the detector that senses changes in the external world (e.g., TRP-4), or the neuromodulator signals that define the internal state of animals (e.g., dopamine and its receptors).
source: Therefore, the diversity of spatial pattern selectivity may arise from variations in either the detector that senses changes in the external world (e.g., TRP-4), or the neuromodulator signals that define the internal state of animals (e.g., dopamine and its receptors).
evidence: Inference from experiments showing both TRP-4 and DOP-3 variations affect behavior.

claim: C. elegans is able to utilize touch sensation to discern different spatial patterns in the environment.

claim: Nematodes can evaluate their environment by sensing food and chemicals.

claim: Touch perception plays a key role in guiding exploration of the physical world in many animal species.

claim: The sense of physical space in C. elegans is highly dynamic and tightly regulated by experience, spatial context, and food availability.

evidence: Summary of multiple experimental findings shown in various figures.

claim: Dopamine may serve as a 'reward' signal that connects the sensation of spatial patterns with innate preferences.

evidence: Speculation based on findings and supported by citation to Schultz et al., 1997.

claim: Dopamine is implicated in spatial attention in higher animals.
source: Nevertheless, together with previous findings implicating dopamine in spatial attention (Bellgrove et al., 2007) and spatial memory (Murphy et al., 1996), as well as in disorders such as agoraphobia in humans (Perna et al., 2011), our study suggests that the coupling between dopamine signaling and a sense of spatial features is an ancestral feature of animal nervous systems.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bellgrove et al., 2007.
